edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Δύο τοίνυν νόμων προκειμένων γενικῶς, καὶ τοῦ μὲν ὄντος τῆς φύσεως νόμου, ὃν θεὸς ἂν νομοθετήσαι, ἑτέρου δὲ τοῦ ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι γραπτοῦ, καλὸν ὅπου μὲν μὴ ἐναντιοῦται ὁ γραπτὸς νόμος τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ μὴ λυπεῖν τοὺς πολίτας προφάσει ξένων νόμων· ἔνθα δὲ τὰ ἐναντία τῷ γραπτῷ νόμῳ προστάσσει ὁ τῆς φύσεως τουτέστι τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅρα εἰ μὴ ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ μακρὰν μὲν χαίρειν εἰπεῖν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις καὶ τῷ βουλήματι τῶν νομοθετῶν, ἐπιδιδόναι δὲ ἑαυτὸν τῷ θεῷ νομοθέτῃ καὶ κατὰ τὸν τούτου λόγον αἱρεῖσθαι βιοῦν, κἂν μετὰ κινδύνων καὶ μυρίων πόνων καὶ θανάτων καὶ ἀδοξίας τοῦτο δέῃ ποιεῖν. καὶ γὰρ ἄτοπον, τῶν ἀρεσκόντων τῷ θεῷ ἑτέρων ὄντων παρὰ τὰ ἀρέσκοντά τισι τῶν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι νόμων, καὶ ἀμηχάνου τυγχάνοντος ἀρέσκειν θεῷ καὶ τοῖς πρεσβεύουσι τοὺς τοιούσδε νόμους, καταφρονεῖν μὲν πράξεων, δι᾿ ὧν ἀρέσει τις τῷ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργῷ, αἱρεῖσθαι δὲ ἐκείνας, ἐξ ὧν ἀπάρεστος μέν τις ἔσται τῷ θεῷ, ἀρεστὸς δὲ τοῖς οὐ νόμοις νόμοις καὶ τοῖς τούτων φίλοις. εἴπερ δὲ εὔλογον ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων τὸν τῆς φύσεως προτιμᾶν νόμον, ὄντα νόμον τοῦ θεοῦ, παρὰ τὸν γεγραμμένον καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐναντίως τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ θεοῦ νενομοθετημένον. πῶς οὐχὶ τοῦτο μᾶλλον ἐν τοῖς περὶ θεοῦ νόμοις ποιητέον; καὶ οὔτε ὡς Αἰθίοπες, [ὡς] οἱ τὰ περὶ τὴν Μερόην οἰκοῦντες, Δία καὶ Διόνυσον, ὡς ἐκείνοις ἀρέσκει, μόνους προσκυνήσομεν, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὅλως Αἰθιοπικοὺς θεοὺς Αἰθιοπικῶς τιμήσομεν· οὔθ᾿ ὡς οἱ Ἀράβιοι τὴν Οὐρανίαν καὶ τὸν Διόνυσον μόνους ἡγησόμεθα θεοὺς, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὅλως θεοὺς. ἐν οἷς τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄῤῥεν δεδόξασται (ὡς θήλειαν γὰρ Ἀράβιοι τὴν Οὐρανίαν προσκυνοῦσι καὶ ὡς ἄῤῥενα τὸν Διόνυσον)· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὡς πάντες Αἰγύπτιοι θεοὺς νομίσομεν Ὄσιριν καὶ Ἶσιν. οὐδὲ τούτοις συγκατατάξομεν κατὰ τὰ τοῖς Σαΐταις (δοκοῦντα) τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν. εἰ δὲ καὶ Ναυκρατίταις ἄλλα μὲν ἔδοξε σέβειν τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις. τὸν Σάραπιν δὲ τοῖς χθὲς καὶ πρώην ἀρξαμένοις. τὸν οὐ πώποτε γενόμενον θεὸν, προσκυνεῖν· οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς νέον τὸν οὐ πρότερον ὄντα θεὸν οὐδὲ γνωσθέντα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις φήσομεν εἶναι. ὁ γὰρ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱὸς, ὁ „πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως,“ εἰ καὶ νεωστὶ ἐνηνθρωπηκέναι ἔδοξεν. ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε διὰ τοῦτο νέος ἐστί. πρεσβύτατον γὰρ αὐτὸν πάντων τῶν δημιουργημάτων ἴσασιν οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι, καὶ αὐτῷ τὸν θεὸν περὶ τῆς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου δημιουργίας εἰρηκέναι· „ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ᾿ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν.“
thought_title: The law of nature stands above written law
pass_a_gloss: Two laws (νόμοι) then being set before [us] generically (γενικῶς), and the one being the law of nature (τῆς φύσεως νόμος), which God would legislate (νομοθετήσαι), the other the written (γραπτός) one in cities (πόλεις), [it is] good, where the written law does not oppose (ἐναντιοῦται) that of God, not to grieve/trouble (λυπεῖν) the citizens (πολῖται) on pretext (προφάσει) of foreign (ξένων) laws; but where the [law] of nature, that is of God, commands (προστάσσει) things contrary to the written law, see whether reason (λόγος) does not require (αἱρεῖ) to say a long farewell (μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπεῖν) to the things written and to the intention (βούλημα) of the lawgivers (νομοθέται), and to give oneself over (ἐπιδιδόναι ἑαυτόν) to God the lawgiver and choose (αἱρεῖσθαι) to live (βιοῦν) according to his word (λόγος), even if with dangers (κίνδυνοι) and countless toils (μυρίοι πόνοι) and deaths (θάνατοι) and disgrace (ἀδοξία) one must do this. For [it is] absurd (ἄτοπον), the things pleasing (ἀρεσκόντων) to God being other than the things pleasing to some of the laws in cities, and it being impossible (ἀμηχάνου) to please God and those upholding/honouring (πρεσβεύουσι) such laws, to despise (καταφρονεῖν) actions (πράξεις) through which one will please the Creator (δημιουργός) of the whole, and to choose those from which one will be displeasing (ἀπάρεστος) to God but pleasing (ἀρεστός) to not-law laws (οὐ νόμοις νόμοις) and to their friends. And if it is reasonable (εὔλογον) in other matters to prefer (προτιμᾶν) the law of nature, being law of God, to the one written and legislated by men contrary to the law of God, how [is it] not rather to be done (ποιητέον) in the laws about God? And neither as Ethiopians, those dwelling around Meroe, will we worship (προσκυνήσομεν) Zeus and Dionysus alone, as pleases them, but not at all will we honour (τιμήσομεν) Ethiopian gods in Ethiopian fashion (Αἰθιοπικῶς); nor as the Arabians will we consider (ἡγησόμεθα) Urania and Dionysus alone gods, but not at all gods, in whom the female (θῆλυ) and the male (ἄρρεν) have been glorified/deemed divine (δεδόξασται) (for Arabians worship Urania as female and Dionysus as male); but neither as all Egyptians will we hold (νομίσομεν) Osiris and Isis gods, nor rank alongside (συγκατατάξομεν) these Athena according to what seems good to the Saites. And if to the Naucratites, to the older ones (πρεσβυτέροις) it seemed good to revere other things, but to those beginning yesterday and the day before (χθὲς καὶ πρώην) to worship Serapis, the one never at any time having become/been (οὐ πώποτε γενόμενον) a god, not for this will we too say that a new (νέον) god exists, not being before nor known to men. For the Son (υἱός) of God, the firstborn of all creation (πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως), even if he seemed recently (νεωστί) to have become man (ἐνηνθρωπηκέναι), yet not at all for this is he new. For the divine words (θεῖοι λόγοι) know (ἴσασιν) him eldest (πρεσβύτατον) of all the created works (δημιουργήματα), and that God said to him about the creation of man (δημιουργία ἀνθρώπου): let us make man according to our image (εἰκών) and likeness (ὁμοίωσις).

pass_b_english: There are, then, two laws set before us in general terms. One is the law of nature, the law God would lay down; the other is the written law in cities. Where the written law does not oppose the law of God, it is right not to trouble the citizens on the pretext of foreign laws. But where the law of nature, that is, of God, commands things contrary to the written law, consider whether reason does not require us to bid a long farewell to what is written and to the intention of the lawgivers, and to give ourselves to God the lawgiver and choose to live according to His word, even if this must be done amid dangers and countless toils, deaths and disgrace.

For it is absurd, when the things that please God are different from those that please some of the laws in cities, and when it is impossible to please both God and those who uphold such laws, to despise the actions by which one will please the Creator of the universe and to choose those by which one will be displeasing to God, but pleasing to laws that are no laws and to their friends. And if in other matters it is reasonable to prefer the law of nature, since it is the law of God, to the law that is written and enacted by men contrary to the law of God, how much more must this be done in the laws that concern God?

So we will not, like the Ethiopians who live around Meroe, worship Zeus and Dionysus alone, as pleases them; no, we will not honour Ethiopian gods in Ethiopian fashion at all. Nor, like the Arabians, will we regard Urania and Dionysus alone as gods; no, we will not regard them as gods at all, gods in whom female and male have been glorified (for the Arabians worship Urania as female and Dionysus as male). Nor will we, like all the Egyptians, hold Osiris and Isis to be gods; nor will we rank Athena with them, as the people of Sais think fit. And if the older people of Naucratis saw fit to revere other objects of worship, while those who began only yesterday or the day before chose to worship Serapis, who never at any time was a god, we will not on that account say, for our part, that there is a new god, one who did not exist before and was not known to men.

For the Son of God, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), even if He was seen to have become man only lately, is not for that reason new. For the divine words know Him as the most ancient of all the works of creation, and know that it was to Him that God said concerning the making of man, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).
notes: ὃν θεὸς ἂν νομοθετήσαι: potential optative, 'the law God would lay down'. κατὰ τὸν τούτου λόγον: 'according to His word' (God's); λόγος could also be 'reason', but the antecedent is God the lawgiver. τοῖς οὐ νόμοις νόμοις: 'laws that are no laws'. The staged Greek prints a bracketed [ὡς] before οἱ τὰ περὶ τὴν Μερόην, which Koetschau deletes; the translation follows the deletion. (δοκοῦντα) after Σαΐταις is an editorial supplement, followed. τὸν οὐ πώποτε γενόμενον θεόν: 'who never at any time was (or became) a god'; Origen denies Serapis divine standing, not historical existence of the cult. εἰ καὶ νεωστὶ ἐνηνθρωπηκέναι ἔδοξεν: ἔδοξεν rendered 'was seen to have become man' rather than 'seemed', to avoid a docetic reading; Origen affirms a real incarnation, and the point is that it appeared to men as recent. πρεσβύτατον αὐτὸν πάντων τῶν δημιουργημάτων: rendered literally 'most ancient of all the works of creation' to keep Origen's own wording; it echoes 'firstborn of all creation' just quoted. Genesis 1:26 quoted from the LXX (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν; the LXX has καθ᾿ ὁμοίωσιν). The phrase 'dangers and countless toils, deaths and disgrace' may faintly echo 2 Corinthians 11:23–26 (ἐν θανάτοις πολλάκις, κινδύνοις), and the whole paragraph the principle of Acts 5:29; neither is a verbal quotation, so neither is cited inline.

Open doubt (review): 5.37: ἔδοξεν is kept as 'was seen to have become man only lately', following the drafter's note against a docetic reading. 'seemed' would be more literal. The owner may want to choose.
